Criminal Defence in Sexual Assault Cases — Pune, Maharashtra

Facing a complaint under Section 63 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023 (BNS 2023) — which replaced Section 376 IPC — is one of the most serious situations a person can encounter in the Indian criminal justice system. Such allegations carry severe stigma, non-bailable offences, and the possibility of life imprisonment. Every accused person has a constitutional right to a fair trial and competent legal representation.

Advocate Akash Chikate provides criminal defence representation in sexual assault matters at Pune District Court, Shivajinagar Court Complex, and the Bombay High Court. This page explains the legal framework, the rights of the accused, and how criminal defence in such matters works.

Important: This page is written from the perspective of defence representation in criminal proceedings. Every accused person is presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond reasonable doubt — this is a fundamental principle of Indian criminal law enshrined in the Constitution.

Relevant BNS 2023 Provisions

SectionOffencePunishment
BNS 63Rape10 years to life imprisonment
BNS 64Rape — aggravated circumstancesMinimum 10 years, up to life
BNS 65Rape — victim under 12 years20 years to life
BNS 66Rape causing death or persistent vegetative state20 years to life or death
BNS 67Gang rape20 years to life
BNS 68Rape by husband — marital rape provision2 to 7 years
BNS 69Sexual intercourse by promise to marry — deceitUp to 10 years
BNS 70Gang rape of woman under 18Life imprisonment
BNS 74Assault or criminal force to womanUp to 2 years
BNS 75Sexual harassmentUp to 3 years
BNS 76Voyeurism1 to 3 years
BNS 77StalkingUp to 3 years

All offences under BNS 63–70 are non-bailable and cognisable. This means police can arrest without a warrant and bail is not a matter of right — it must be argued and granted by a court.

Bail in Sexual Assault Cases

Because these offences are non-bailable, bail requires a formal application before a Judicial Magistrate First Class (JMFC) or Sessions Court. Courts consider:

  • Nature and gravity of the accusation
  • Antecedents of the accused (prior criminal record)
  • Risk of the accused absconding
  • Risk of tampering with evidence or influencing witnesses
  • Medical evidence on record
  • Prior relationship between accused and complainant

Anticipatory bail is available under Section 482 BNSS before arrest in cases where a complaint has been filed but no arrest has been made.

Common Defence Arguments in Sexual Assault Cases

1. Consent

Where the allegation arises from a consensual relationship, the defence examines communications (messages, call records), prior meetings, photographs, and the nature of the relationship.

2. Promise to Marry Disputes (BNS 69)

BNS 69 criminalises sexual intercourse obtained by deceitful promise of marriage. Courts have held that a bona fide promise that later could not be fulfilled does not automatically constitute the offence — the prosecution must prove the promise was false from the inception.

3. Delay in Filing FIR

An unexplained delay of weeks or months in filing the FIR is a factor courts weigh. Unexplained delay requires explanation by the prosecution.

4. Medical Evidence

Where medical records are inconsistent with the complainant's account, this is a significant defence point.

5. Contradictions in Statement

The complainant's Section 164 BNSS statement, the FIR, and trial evidence are examined for material contradictions.

6. Motive to Falsely Implicate

In cases arising from failed relationships, property disputes, or personal enmity, the defence examines whether there is a demonstrable motive for a false complaint.

7. Alibi

Where the accused was provably in a different location at the time of the incident, alibi evidence supported by documentary proof constitutes a complete defence.

Special Court Procedure in Pune

  • Trial must be completed within 2 months (target under law — in practice longer)
  • In-camera proceedings to protect the complainant's identity
  • Complainant's identity cannot be disclosed publicly
  • Section 53A BNS: character evidence regarding past sexual history is inadmissible
  • Video conferencing of complainant's evidence is possible

Digital Evidence in Sexual Assault Cases

Under BPSS 2023, digital evidence plays a significant role. Defence examines authenticity of digital evidence, whether messages are presented in complete context, chain of custody of devices, and whether digital forensics was conducted properly.

Protecting Your Rights — Immediate Steps

  1. Do not make any statement to police without legal counsel present
  2. Contact a criminal defence lawyer immediately — before any arrest if possible
  3. Preserve all relevant evidence — messages, call logs, photographs, travel records
  4. Do not contact the complainant or any potential witness
  5. Consider anticipatory bail if arrest is anticipated — Section 482 BNSS

Frequently Asked Questions

Is bail available in rape cases in India?

Bail in rape cases (BNS 63 and related sections) is not a matter of right — it must be argued before a Sessions Court or Bombay High Court. Bail is possible but requires strong grounds and effective legal representation.

What is the difference between BNS 63 and BNS 69?

BNS 63 covers rape in all its forms. BNS 69 specifically covers sexual intercourse by deceitful means including a false promise of marriage. Courts have held that BNS 69 requires proof that the promise was false from the beginning.

Can anticipatory bail be obtained in a rape case?

Anticipatory bail under Section 482 BNSS can be applied for before arrest. Courts apply a higher standard of scrutiny in sexual offence matters. Whether granted depends on the specific facts and grounds presented.

How long does a rape trial take in Pune?

While the law mandates completion within 2 months, in practice rape trials at Pune Special Courts take significantly longer due to caseload.

What is the role of defence counsel in a rape trial?

Defence counsel ensures the accused receives a fair trial, that the prosecution proves its case beyond reasonable doubt, that evidence is properly admitted under BPSS 2023, and that the accused's constitutional rights are protected throughout.

item.dc:creator: admin

Murder and Culpable Homicide Defence Lawyer — Pune, Maharashtra

An accusation of murder under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023 (BNS 2023) is the gravest criminal charge an individual can face. It carries the possibility of life imprisonment or the death penalty. From the moment of arrest, every procedural step matters.

Advocate Akash Chikate provides criminal defence representation in murder and culpable homicide matters at Pune District Court, Shivajinagar Court Complex, and the Bombay High Court. With 8+ years of criminal law practice and 27+ Bombay High Court orders, Advocate Chikate understands the procedural rigour these cases demand.

BNS 2023 — Homicide Provisions

SectionOffencePunishment
BNS 100Culpable homicide not amounting to murderUp to 10 years, or life
BNS 101MurderDeath or life imprisonment + fine
BNS 102Murder by life-convictDeath
BNS 103Punishment for murderDeath or life imprisonment
BNS 104Culpable homicide — reduced punishment10 years or life
BNS 105Causing death by negligenceUp to 5 years
BNS 106Causing death by negligence (rash driving)Up to 10 years
BNS 107Abetment of suicideUp to 10 years
BNS 108Attempt to murderUp to 10 years; life if hurt caused
BNS 109Attempt to commit culpable homicideUp to 3 years

All offences under BNS 101-109 are non-bailable and cognisable.

The Critical Distinction: Murder vs. Culpable Homicide

Murder (BNS 101) requires:

  • Intention to cause death, OR
  • Intention to cause bodily injury likely to cause death, OR
  • Knowledge that the act is imminently dangerous and likely to cause death

Culpable homicide not amounting to murder applies where:

  • The act was done under grave and sudden provocation
  • The accused exceeded the right of private defence
  • The accused acted in the heat of passion without premeditation
  • The knowledge of causing death was present but not the intention

This distinction — which can mean the difference between the death penalty and 10 years imprisonment — is what skilled defence counsel argues in every homicide case.

Bail in Murder Cases

Murder under BNS 101 is non-bailable. Bail must be sought from the Sessions Court (first application) or the Bombay High Court if Sessions Court rejects.

Factors courts consider:

  • Prima facie strength of prosecution case
  • Nature of the evidence (eyewitness, circumstantial, forensic)
  • Criminal antecedents of the accused
  • Risk of absconding
  • Period of custody already undergone
  • Whether trial is proceeding or delayed
  • Role of the specific accused (main accused vs. co-accused)

Key Defence Strategies in Homicide Cases

1. Right of Private Defence (BNS 34–44)

Where death occurred while the accused was defending themselves or another person from an assault, the right of private defence is a complete defence. Where the force used was excessive, the offence may be reduced to culpable homicide under BNS 104.

2. Sudden Grave Provocation

Where the act was committed in the heat of passion following sudden grave provocation, without premeditation, the offence is reduced from murder to culpable homicide not amounting to murder.

3. Challenging Eyewitness Testimony

Defence examines: whether the witness had clear visibility, lighting conditions, distance from the incident, motive to falsely identify the accused, and whether the identification was properly conducted (Test Identification Parade).

4. Forensic Evidence Challenges

Post-mortem reports, ballistic reports, blood grouping, DNA, and fingerprint analysis can be challenged on methodology of collection, chain of custody, qualification of the forensic expert, and consistency with the prosecution's case theory.

5. Alibi

Where the accused was provably elsewhere at the time of the incident, alibi evidence supported by CCTV footage, digital location data, ticket records, or credible witness testimony provides a complete defence.

6. Circumstantial Evidence — Last Seen Theory

Courts require that the chain of circumstances is complete and consistent only with the guilt of the accused. Defence identifies any gaps in the chain.

7. Co-Accused — Specific Role

In cases with multiple accused, defence examines whether the specific client had the common intention required under BNS 3(5). Liability does not attach to every co-accused automatically.

Procedure — Murder Trial in Pune

  1. FIR registered at local police station
  2. Investigation — panchanama, spot inspection, post-mortem, forensic samples
  3. Chargesheet filed before Judicial Magistrate within 60/90 days
  4. Committal to Sessions Court (murder is exclusively triable by Sessions Court)
  5. Charges framed by Sessions Court
  6. Prosecution evidence — examination of witnesses, documents, forensic reports
  7. Defence evidence — accused's statement under Section 351 BNSS, defence witnesses
  8. Arguments by prosecution and defence
  9. Judgment — conviction or acquittal
  10. Appeal to Bombay High Court if convicted

Frequently Asked Questions

Can bail be obtained in a murder case in Pune?

Bail in murder cases (BNS 101) is not a matter of right. Grounds include: weak prosecution evidence, long pre-trial custody, the accused's specific limited role, and delay in trial. It is difficult but not impossible.

What is the difference between murder and attempt to murder?

Murder (BNS 101) requires that death has actually occurred. Attempt to murder (BNS 108) applies where the accused, with intent to cause death, does an act that falls short of causing death. Attempt to murder carries up to 10 years, and up to life if hurt is actually caused.

What is culpable homicide not amounting to murder?

Culpable homicide not amounting to murder (BNS 100) applies where death was caused without full murderous intent — for example, under sudden grave provocation, or where the accused exceeded the right of private defence. The punishment is up to 10 years or life imprisonment.

Is the death penalty given in murder cases in Maharashtra?

The death penalty is imposed only in the "rarest of rare" cases. Most murder convictions result in life imprisonment. Both the Sessions Court and the Bombay High Court must agree before execution.

What should I do if I am accused of murder?

Contact a criminal defence lawyer immediately. Do not make any statement to police without counsel present. If not yet arrested, consider anticipatory bail. Preserve any evidence that supports your account of events.

PMLA / Money Laundering Defence Lawyer — Pune, Maharashtra

The Prevention of Money Laundering Act 2002 (PMLA) gives the Enforcement Directorate (ED) sweeping powers to investigate, arrest, attach property, and prosecute. A PMLA case often begins with an ED notice or raid — and the consequences move quickly: bank accounts frozen, property attached, and arrest without the procedural protections available in ordinary criminal matters.

Advocate Akash Chikate provides criminal defence in PMLA matters in Pune, including ED summons response, PMLA bail applications, attachment challenges, and representation before Special PMLA Courts and the Bombay High Court.

What is Money Laundering Under PMLA?

Under Section 3 of the PMLA, money laundering occurs when a person directly or indirectly attempts to indulge in, or assists, or is a party to, or is actually involved in any process or activity connected with the proceeds of crime — including concealment, possession, acquisition, use, projection as untainted, or claiming as untainted property.

Punishment under PMLA Section 4: Rigorous imprisonment of 3 to 7 years, extendable to 10 years where the Scheduled Offence is under NDPS Act.

The ED Investigation Process

Stage 1: Predicate Offence FIR

PMLA investigation always traces back to a predicate offence — typically an FIR under BNS for cheating, fraud, corruption, NDPS, etc. Once ED registers an Enforcement Case Information Report (ECIR), it runs parallel to the police investigation.

Stage 2: Summons / Notice Under Section 50 PMLA

ED issues summons requiring appearance for statement recording. These are not optional — failure to appear can lead to arrest. Statements recorded under Section 50 are admissible as evidence (unlike police statements under BNSS).

Stage 3: Search and Seizure

ED can conduct searches and seize documents, digital devices, cash, and property under Section 17 PMLA.

Stage 4: Provisional Attachment

ED can provisionally attach property (bank accounts, real estate, vehicles) under Section 5 PMLA. Attachment can occur even before arrest.

Stage 5: Arrest

ED can arrest under Section 19 PMLA if it has reason to believe the person is guilty of money laundering.

Stage 6: Adjudicating Authority and Special Court

The ED's attachment is confirmed or rejected by the Adjudicating Authority (PMLA). Criminal prosecution is before Special Courts constituted under Section 43 PMLA.

PMLA Bail — Why It Is Difficult

Section 45 PMLA imposes a twin condition bail test. Before granting bail, the court must be satisfied that:

  1. There are reasonable grounds for believing the accused is not guilty of the offence, AND
  2. The accused is not likely to commit any offence while on bail

Grounds that have succeeded in PMLA bail:

  • Prosecution failing to demonstrate proceeds of crime traceable to the accused
  • Predicate offence itself is weak or being challenged
  • Accused has cooperated with investigation
  • Long custody without meaningful trial progress
  • Medical grounds

Challenging Property Attachment

ED's provisional attachment under Section 5 PMLA can be challenged before the Adjudicating Authority and the PMLA Appellate Tribunal. Grounds include:

  • Property does not constitute proceeds of crime
  • Property was acquired from legitimate sources prior to any alleged offence
  • The predicate offence itself is under challenge or has been quashed
  • Property belongs to a bona fide third party with no nexus to the alleged offence
  • Procedural non-compliance in attachment order

Defence Strategies in PMLA Cases

1. Attack the Predicate Offence

PMLA cannot stand if the predicate (Scheduled) offence is quashed, discharged, or acquitted. If the underlying FIR is successfully challenged under Section 528 BNSS, the PMLA proceeding is significantly weakened.

2. No Proceeds of Crime

The prosecution must establish that the accused received or dealt with "proceeds of crime" traceable to the Scheduled Offence. Where the money trail is absent or demonstrates legitimate transactions, the PMLA case weakens.

3. Section 50 Statement Challenges

Defence examines whether the statement was voluntarily made, properly recorded, and not coerced.

4. KYC and Documentary Paper Trail

Where transactions were properly documented, bank-certified, and tax-compliant, a clean paper trail is one of the strongest defences.

Key Differences: ED vs. Police Investigation

AspectPolice (BNSS)ED (PMLA)
Statement admissibilityNot admissible as evidenceAdmissible as evidence (Section 50)
Bail standardStandard BNSS factorsTwin conditions (Section 45)
Property attachmentCourt order requiredED provisional attachment (Section 5)
Chargesheet deadline60/90 daysNo fixed statutory deadline
RemandPolice/judicial remandED custody remand
Case informationFIR publicECIR not public

Frequently Asked Questions

I received an ED summons under PMLA. Must I appear?

Yes. Summons under Section 50 PMLA must be complied with. Failure to appear without reasonable cause can lead to ED arrest. Before appearing, consult a criminal defence lawyer. You have the right to have counsel present during questioning.

Can ED arrest without a court warrant?

Yes. Under Section 19 PMLA, the ED can arrest a person if there are reasons to believe they are guilty of money laundering. No court warrant is required for the arrest itself.

My bank account has been frozen by ED. What can I do?

ED provisional attachment of bank accounts under Section 5 PMLA must be confirmed by the Adjudicating Authority within 60 days. You can challenge the attachment before the Adjudicating Authority and, if unsuccessful, before the PMLA Appellate Tribunal and the Bombay High Court.

Is PMLA bail possible?

PMLA bail under Section 45 is subject to twin conditions. It is more difficult than standard bail but has been granted in cases with weak evidence, long custody, or strong defence grounds.

Prevention of Corruption Act (PC Act) Defence Lawyer — Pune, Maharashtra

The Prevention of Corruption Act 1988 (as amended 2018) governs the prosecution of public servants and those who pay bribes. In Maharashtra, PC Act cases are investigated by the Anti-Corruption Bureau (ACB), the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI), and the Enforcement Directorate (ED) for the money laundering angle.

Advocate Akash Chikate provides criminal defence in PC Act matters in Pune, including ACB trap case defence, CBI matter representation, bail applications, and proceedings before the Special Court (PC Act) and Bombay High Court.

Key Provisions — PC Act 1988 (as amended 2018)

SectionOffencePunishment
PC Act 7Public servant accepting gratification (bribe)3 to 7 years + fine
PC Act 7ATaking undue advantage to influence public servant3 to 7 years + fine
PC Act 8Bribe-giver (giving gratification)7 years + fine
PC Act 9Bribe through a commercial organisation7 years + fine
PC Act 11Public servant obtaining valuables without consideration3 to 7 years + fine
PC Act 13(1)(b)Disproportionate assets7 years + fine
PC Act 17AInvestigation sanction requirementProsecution sanction needed

All PC Act offences are cognisable and non-bailable. Trial occurs before Special Courts designated under the PC Act.

The 2018 Amendment — Critical Changes

  1. Bribe-giving is now a criminal offence (Section 8): The person who pays a bribe is also liable (3–7 years). Exception: if the person was compelled to pay and reports it to law enforcement within 7 days.
  2. Section 17A — Prosecution Sanction: Before any investigation of a public servant for acts done in official capacity, the investigating agency must obtain sanction from the competent government authority. Failure to obtain prior sanction is a ground to challenge the entire investigation.
  3. Disproportionate Assets (Section 13(1)(b)): A public servant possessing assets disproportionate to their known sources of income is guilty of criminal misconduct.

ACB Trap Cases — How They Work

  1. Complaint: A complainant approaches ACB alleging a public servant demanded a bribe.
  2. Trap preparation: ACB prepares trap currency (phenolphthalein powder applied to notes).
  3. Trap laid: The complainant pays the bribe with the prepared notes in ACB's presence.
  4. Arrest: ACB apprehends the public servant; hands test positive for phenolphthalein.
  5. Panchanama: ACB records a detailed panchanama of the trap proceedings.
  6. FIR and prosecution: ACB registers FIR and files chargesheet before Special Court.

Defence in ACB Trap Cases

1. Demand Not Established

Section 7 PC Act requires proof that the accused demanded the gratification — not merely that they received it. The absence of independent corroboration of demand is a significant defence point.

2. No Voluntary Acceptance

If the currency was thrust upon the accused or placed near them without their knowledge, mere possession of trap currency without voluntary acceptance does not establish the offence.

3. Phenolphthalein Test — Contamination

The phenolphthalein test can produce false positives from contact with other substances. Defence examines the test procedure, chain of custody of the trap currency, and whether the panchanama records are consistent.

4. Complainant's Motive

ACB complaints are sometimes motivated by personal enmity, vendetta, or to escape legitimate government action. A demonstrable motive for a false complaint is material to the defence.

5. Independent Witness Issues

ACB traps require independent witnesses (panchas). Where the panchas are police department employees or have prior ACB involvement, their independence can be challenged.

6. Section 17A — Sanction Absence

Prior sanction under Section 17A PC Act is mandatory before investigation. Absence of proper sanction is a ground to challenge the prosecution.

Disproportionate Assets (DA) Cases

Key defence arguments in DA cases:

  • Income from legitimate sources not accounted for by prosecution (agricultural income, inherited property, gifts)
  • Gifts and inheritances properly documented
  • Assets belong to family members with independent income sources
  • Valuation of property challenged
  • Known sources of income not correctly calculated by prosecution
  • Calculation period challenged

Bail in PC Act Cases

Factors favouring bail in PC Act matters:

  • Accused is a first-time offender with no criminal history
  • The trap case evidence has specific procedural defects
  • Accused has cooperated with investigation
  • Long custody period without trial completion
  • Prosecution sanction under Section 17A obtained improperly

Frequently Asked Questions

Is paying a bribe a criminal offence?

Yes — since the 2018 PC Act amendment, Section 8 makes bribe-giving a criminal offence punishable with up to 7 years imprisonment. Exception: if a person was compelled to give a bribe and voluntarily reports it to law enforcement within 7 days.

What is the Section 17A sanction and why does it matter?

Section 17A PC Act requires prior sanction from the competent government authority before investigating a public servant for acts done in their official capacity. If the investigating agency proceeded without sanction, the entire investigation and prosecution may be liable to be quashed.

Can a PC Act case be quashed at Bombay High Court?

Yes — PC Act cases can be quashed under Section 528 BNSS on grounds including: absence of sanction under Section 17A, no demand established on the face of the FIR, mala fide complaint, or where the prosecution case is inherently improbable.

What is an ACB trap case?

An ACB (Anti-Corruption Bureau) trap case is a sting operation where the ACB, acting on a complaint, prepares marked currency and facilitates payment of a demanded bribe to catch a public servant red-handed. The trap is documented in a panchanama by ACB officers and independent witnesses.

I am a government servant who received currency without demanding it. What should I do?

Contact a criminal defence lawyer immediately. Do not make any statement to ACB or police without counsel. Whether you demanded the currency is a central question in the prosecution — your defence must be carefully structured from the outset.

How long do PC Act trials take in Pune?

PC Act trials before the Special Court in Pune typically take 3–8 years from chargesheet to judgment. Bail during the trial period is therefore particularly important.
